notes.meaning: King Xerxes cooled down after his angry outburst against Queen Vashti. He remembered her with deep regret, but Persian royal law prevented him from taking her back. Even in this difficult situation, God was silently directing events toward His own plan to rescue His people.

The king's personal attendants worried he might change his mind and punish them, so they suggested gathering beautiful young women from every province. These maidens were brought to the palace harem to receive special beauty treatments before meeting the king. The woman who pleased him most would be chosen as the new queen in place of Vashti.

A Jewish man named Mordecai lived in the fortress city of Susa. He came from the tribe of Benjamin and served in an official role near the king's palace. God placed him close to the seat of power long before trouble arose.

Mordecai's ancestors had been forced out of Jerusalem when the king of Babylon captured the city and took King Jeconiah away. Even though this family lived far away in exile, they kept their Jewish identity. God never lost sight of His scattered people.

Mordecai had raised his orphaned younger cousin, Hadassah, who was also known by her Persian name, Esther. She was very lovely, and when her parents died, Mordecai welcomed her into his home as his own daughter. God used his loving family care to protect and prepare her.

When the king's royal decree was announced, many young women were taken to the palace in Susa. Esther was taken along with them and placed in the care of Hegai, the royal officer in charge of the harem. She had to submit to the king's sweeping royal order.

Esther quickly won the favor and goodwill of Hegai because of her humble and gracious conduct. He hurried to provide her beauty supplies, special food, and seven trained maidservants, moving her to the best quarters in the harem. God gave her kindness and respect in the eyes of this royal supervisor.

Esther did not reveal her Jewish family or heritage because Mordecai had carefully instructed her to keep it quiet. This careful silence protected her from palace prejudice and kept her safe in a pagan environment. God guided this discretion for a purpose that would become clear later.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters argue that hiding her Jewish identity showed a lack of religious commitment compared to heroes like Daniel.

notes.meaning: Mordecai walked past the courtyard of the harem every single day to ask how Esther was doing. He watched over her safety with the steady love of a faithful father. His constant concern shows how deeply devoted he remained to the girl he had raised.

Each young woman went through a full twelve months of preparation before her appointment with the king. The first six months were spent using oil of myrrh, followed by six months of sweet perfumes and special lotions. This long routine followed Persian court rules to clean and fragrance each woman thoroughly.

When a woman was finally called to meet the king, she was allowed to take whatever dresses or jewelry she wanted from the women's quarters. Everything she chose was handed to her so she could dress according to her own taste. Most women piled on luxuries to try to catch the king's eye.

A maiden went to the king in the evening and was sent the next morning to a second harem managed by Shaashgaz. From that point on, she lived as a secondary wife and would never visit the king again unless he called for her by name. This shows the lonely, confined life that waited for women in the royal Persian system.

When Esther's turn came, she did not ask for extra jewelry or fancy robes, taking only what Hegai advised. Her simple modesty and natural charm won the admiration of everyone who saw her. She trusted wise counsel rather than trying to impress people with outward display.

Esther was brought into King Xerxes' royal palace in the tenth month, called Tebeth, during the seventh year of his reign. About four years had passed since Vashti had been removed from her position. God brought Esther before the ruler at just the right moment in history.

King Xerxes loved Esther far more than all the other women, and she won his deepest affection. He set the royal crown upon her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. God lifted an orphan exile from the dust to the highest royal seat in the empire.

The king hosted a great celebration called Esther's banquet for all his nobles and officials. He also gave the provinces relief from taxes and distributed lavish royal gifts to honor his new queen. The entire kingdom shared in the celebration of Esther's crowning.

While young women were gathered a second time, Mordecai sat on duty at the king's palace gate. Sitting at the gate meant he held a trusted post in the royal court system. He faithfully carried out his daily duties without seeking public glory.

Even after becoming queen, Esther continued to keep her family background secret, just as Mordecai had told her. She respected and obeyed his instructions exactly as she had done when growing up in his home. Her humble loyalty kept her grounded despite her high new rank.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Old Testament includes Greek additions to this verse stating that Mordecai ordered Esther to fear God and keep His commandments while living in the royal house.

notes.meaning: While Mordecai was stationed at the palace gate, two royal doorkeepers named Bigthan and Teresh grew angry and plotted to murder the king. Mordecai learned about the conspiracy and passed the news to Queen Esther, who then warned the king in Mordecai's name. Mordecai acted as an honest citizen by protecting the life of the ruler over him.

The palace officials looked into the report, confirmed the assassination plot, and executed both traitors by hanging them on wooden stakes. The whole event was written down in the royal record book right before the king. Mordecai received no immediate reward, but God made sure his good deed was recorded for the future.
